level1.text: The pressure of a gas in a closed rigid container follows the line $p = 98.0\,\text{kPa} + 0.360\,\tfrac{\text{kPa}}{{}^\circ\text{C}} \cdot \theta$ within the measurement range, where $\theta$ is the temperature in degrees Celsius. At what temperature does the line give a pressure of zero? Give your answer in degrees Celsius.
The pressure of a gas in a closed container is 105.0 kPa at 20.0 °C and 127.0 kPa at 80.0 °C. Calculate the slope of the line through these points in the unit kPa/°C.

A group of students obtained the value $-267.90\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ for absolute zero by extrapolation. By how many degrees Celsius does the result differ from the accepted value $-273.15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$?

Of the two limit lines drawn through the measurement points, the steeper meets zero pressure at the temperature $-258\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and the shallower at $-284\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How large is the uncertainty of the result $\Delta\theta_0$?
The pressure gauge reading is 112 kPa, and the uncertainty of the gauge is $\pm 1.0\,\text{kPa}$. What percentage of the reading is the uncertainty?

level2.text: The pressure of the air in a flask was measured at two temperatures: at 15.0 °C the pressure was 1.050 bar and at 95.0 °C it was 1.360 bar. Assume that the pressure depends linearly on temperature. At what temperature does the line give zero pressure? Give your answer in degrees Celsius.

Two limit lines can be drawn through the measurement points of the gas pressure: $p = 100\,\text{kPa} + 0.380\,\tfrac{\text{kPa}}{{}^\circ\text{C}} \cdot \theta$ and $p = 102\,\text{kPa} + 0.350\,\tfrac{\text{kPa}}{{}^\circ\text{C}} \cdot \theta$. Calculate the temperature at zero pressure for each line and use them to find the uncertainty of absolute zero $\Delta\theta_0$.

In the experiment, a pressure gauge was used that shows the gauge pressure compared with the surrounding atmospheric pressure. The atmospheric pressure was 101.0 kPa. The gauge reading was 9.0 kPa at 30.0 °C and 31.0 kPa at 90.0 °C. At what temperature would the absolute pressure of the gas be zero, when the pressure depends linearly on temperature? Give your answer in degrees Celsius.

In the experiment, the reading precision of the temperature is $\pm 0.50\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ and of the pressure $\pm 1.0\,\text{kPa}$. The slope of the line through the measurement points is $0.36\,\tfrac{\text{kPa}}{{}^\circ\text{C}}$. On the line, the temperature uncertainty $\pm 0.50\,{}^\circ\text{C}$ corresponds to a certain change in pressure. What percentage of the pressure uncertainty $1.0\,\text{kPa}$ is this change in pressure?

level3.text: The measurement range is 20.0–100.0 °C. At 20.0 °C the pressure is $106.0 \pm 1.0\,\text{kPa}$ and at 100.0 °C it is $137.0 \pm 1.0\,\text{kPa}$. The steepest limit line passes through the points (20.0 °C; 105.0 kPa) and (100.0 °C; 138.0 kPa), and the shallowest through the points (20.0 °C; 107.0 kPa) and (100.0 °C; 136.0 kPa). Determine the uncertainty of absolute zero $\Delta\theta_0$ and deduce why limit lines based on the end points alone give a larger uncertainty than the seven-point data.

The pressure of nitrogen gas in a rigid container is 100.0 kPa at 0 °C, and the pressure is directly proportional to the temperature in kelvins. What pressure would the line give at 77.0 K, where nitrogen boils at normal pressure? At such a low pressure, nitrogen gas condenses into a liquid only at about 67 K. Justify why the line cannot be extended all the way to absolute zero. Give your answer as a pressure in kilopascals.

The result of group A's measurement is $\theta_0 = -262.00 \pm 6.00\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. The accepted value is $-273.15\,{}^\circ\text{C}$. How many times does the uncertainty $\Delta\theta_0$ fit between the result and the accepted value? Deduce a reason why the result does not agree with the accepted value.
